newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German electronics face sluggish 1997 - ZVEI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German electronics face sluggish 1997 - ZVEI.

text.p: Dim prospects for the German economy in 1997 has left the electronics industry to face another year with growth of no more than two percent, the ZVEI industry association warned on Thursday.
Hopes which flickered earlier this year for an economic recovery on the crucial home market in the second half of 1996 had not been fulfilled, the ZVEI told a news conference.
"Once again our hopes are therefore pinned on exports," said managing director Franz-Josef Wissing, adding that even here, recent strong growth rates were expected to level off.

The ZVEI, which represents German electronics giants such as Siemens AG, said robust export business and strong demand for communications and information technologies had led to two percent growth in sales and output this year.

Exports showed a six percent rise to 57 billion marks in the first half of 1996, amid advances of as much as 20 percent in developing markets of South East Asia, eastern Europe and Latin America, but ZVEI cautioned that these growth rates were not guaranteed to continue.

Wissing said more needed to be done to improve German firms' foreign status, especially since the global electronics industry was expected to grow by seven percent a year on average through the year 2000.

"Germany may have generally a top position in the European electronics markets...but in the fast-growing markets like South East Asia...and the NAFTA countries, Germany's shares of imports are still just between one and five percent."

But the main depressant for the industry was the disappointing home market, where demand for household- and entertainment-related equipment, and from the beleaguered building sector, was particularly sluggish.

The ZVEI said overall industry sales had risen 1.8 percent to 169.5 billion marks in the first nine months of 1996, but domestic sales, which account for two-thirds of the total, were static. Full year output should be about 226 billion marks.
"There are no indications of any improvement on the German market and that is a prerequisite for lasting growth," Wissing said. "Incoming orders were down about 0.5 percent this year."
The group did not release profit figures but said the overall earnings picture among German firms remained "unsatisfactory".
Wissing said profits were being minimised by continued competitive and price pressures. Moreover, despite the job cuts, capacity utilisation increased only marginally to 82 percent from 81.5 percent.

High wage costs and a growing trend to shift production abroad were continuing to spark jobs cuts throughout Germany. By the end of September, employment had dropped by 24,000 to 884,000 and a total of 30,000 would be lost by year-end.
Wissing said the German electronics industry had obvious strengths, such as energy-related products, telecoms, industrial automation parts and vehicle technology.
The clear weaknesses, on an international level, were developing highly cost-sensitive products for the mass market, such as entertainment electronics.
